screens.title: Ingesting Real‑time Data with Azure Event Hubs
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you’ll master practical techniques for sending and receiving streams with Azure Event Hubs. We’ll cover portal configuration so you have a namespace and an Event Hub ready, then build a Python producer that sends JSON payloads efficiently using batching and partition keys. You will also learn how to write a consumer that uses checkpointing and Blob storage so processing can resume after failures. We’ll explain EventProcessorClient and BlobCheckpointStore for load balanced, fault tolerant consumption, and how Event Hubs Capture archives raw events to Azure Storage in Avro or Parquet format. Throughout, I’ll show concrete examples, common mistakes to avoid — like sending tiny unbatched events or failing to checkpoint — and simple remedies. By the end you will understand the end-to-end flow from device telemetry to archive, why ordering matters for device streams, and how to make your consumers resilient. Think about one stream you will build: how will you guarantee ordering and restart safely after a crash?

screens.title: Create an Event Hubs Namespace and Event Hub
screens.narratorSegment: Creating an Event Hubs namespace and an Event Hub in the portal is the foundation for reliable ingestion. Start by selecting or creating a resource group, then create an Event Hubs namespace; choose the pricing and throughput options that match expected traffic. When you create the Event Hub inside the namespace pick an appropriate partition count because partitions determine parallelism and ordering domains. A higher partition count allows more concurrent readers, but partitions are fixed after creation, so plan for future scaling. After provisioning, retrieve the namespace connection string from the Shared access policies section and copy it securely. For checkpointing you will also prepare a Storage account and container to hold checkpoint blobs. One common misconception is that partitions are dynamic— they are not; resizing requires a new Event Hub and data migration strategy. A concrete example: if a telemetry system will have many independent device streams that need parallel consumer processing, plan for several partitions; if ordering per device is required, use deviceId as a partition key rather than increasing partitions. Key takeaway: choose partitions and throughput with future scaling and ordering requirements in mind.

Step-by-step portal flow

Common misconception
Partitions are not elastic. You cannot change partition count after creating the Event Hub. Instead, plan ahead or create a new Event Hub and migrate data if scale needs grow.

screens.title: Connection Strings, Security, and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: A connection string contains the endpoint and authentication credentials that let your producer and consumer talk to an Event Hub. It is convenient for development, but in production storing that string directly in code is a common security mistake. Instead, use Azure Key Vault to store secrets or, where supported, use a managed identity so your application requests tokens without handling raw keys. When you copy a connection string from the portal you will typically use a policy such as RootManageSharedAccessKey for testing, but production systems should use least privilege policies scoped to send or listen. As an example, a producer app can retrieve a connection string from Key Vault at startup and then open an EventHubProducerClient from that connection string. Another misconception is thinking managed identities replace all configuration; they replace secret storage but your application still needs the Event Hub name and consumer group configuration. Key takeaway: protect your connection information, rotate keys when needed, and apply least privilege for better security posture. Connection Strings, Security, and Best Practices means use key vault or managed identities; avoid embedding namespace keys in application code and prefer least-privilege policies.. In practical terms, how to provide credentials to producers and consumers securely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Connection & Security
Connection string essentials
The connection string contains the service endpoint and a shared access key. For production use least privilege policies and never hardcode the connection string in source control.
Secure storage options
  • Azure Key Vault: store and rotate keys, retrieve at runtime.
  • Managed Identity: avoid secrets by using Azure AD tokens when supported by your SDK.
  • Scoped SAS policies: grant only Send or Listen as needed.
Key Takeaway
Protect connection strings with Key Vault or managed identities and use least privilege for access policies.
Quick example: secret retrieval (concept)
# Application retrieves secret from Key Vault once at startup, then constructs EventHubProducerClient with it.
Misconception
Using RootManageSharedAccessKey everywhere is common in quick demos, but it grants management-level permissions. Prefer separate Send and Listen policies in production.

screens.title: Producer: Sending Events in Python with Batching
screens.narratorSegment: This code walkthrough demonstrates a practical Python producer that sends telemetry events in batches. The producer opens an EventHubProducerClient from a connection string and creates EventData objects by serializing dictionaries to JSON. Best practice is to create batches with create_batch and add events to the batch before sending. Batching reduces per-event network overhead and improves throughput. The partition key is set so related events, for example those from the same deviceId, are guaranteed to land in the same partition and preserve ordering. A typical pattern simulates multiple devices and uses the device identifier as the partition key property. One misconception is setting partition keys on different events expecting cross-device ordering; partition keys only guarantee ordering within the same key value. In production, you should also handle retries and backoff and avoid blocking the event loop in async apps. The example illustrates these principles and gives you a direct template to adapt for real telemetry producers. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Producer: Python
Python producer (async) — key sections
import asyncio
from azure.eventhub.aio import EventHubProducerClient
from azure.eventhub import EventData
import json, random, datetime

EVENT_HUB_CONNECTION_STR = "Endpoint=sb://<your-namespace>.servicebus.windows.net/;SharedAccessKeyName=RootManageSharedAccessKey;SharedAccessKey=<your-key>"
EVENT_HUB_NAME = "telemetry-events"

async def run():
  producer = EventHubProducerClient.from_connection_string(
    conn_str=EVENT_HUB_CONNECTION_STR,
    eventhub_name=EVENT_HUB_NAME
  )
  async with producer:
    for i in range(10):
      device_id = f"device-{random.randint(1,3)}"
      event_payload = {
        "deviceId": device_id,
        "temperature": round(random.uniform(20.0,30.0),2),
        "timestamp": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
      }
      event_data = EventData(json.dumps(event_payload))
      event_data.properties = {"partition_key": device_id}
      event_batch = await producer.create_batch()
      event_batch.add(event_data)
      await producer.send_batch(event_batch)
      await asyncio.sleep(1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
  asyncio.run(run())
This snippet shows serializing a payload to JSON, creating EventData, setting a partition key, batching, and sending. Adapt the batch loop to add multiple events per batch for higher throughput.
Notes & example
  • Set partition_key to deviceId to preserve ordering per device.
  • Send multiple EventData items in one batch to reduce RPC overhead.
  • Handle retries and backoff in production to manage transient failures.
Common mistake
Sending many single‑event sends increases overhead and reduces throughput. Batch related events where possible.

screens.title: Partition Key and Event Ordering
screens.narratorSegment: Partition keys are the mechanism that routes related events to the same partition so they are processed in order. When you set a partition key, all events with the same key are guaranteed to be written to the same partition, maintaining sequence within that partition. This is essential for scenarios like device telemetry where the sequence of sensor readings matters. For example, using deviceId as a partition key ensures all events from a single device appear in arrival order on the same partition. A common misconception is that a partition key enforces global ordering across the Event Hub; it does not. Ordering is only guaranteed within a partition for identical partition keys. Also remember that partitions are fixed at Event Hub creation, so partition keys must be chosen considering partition count: if you have more distinct keys than partitions, multiple keys will map into the same partition using a hashing mechanism. Key takeaway: use partition keys to preserve ordering for related streams and choose partition counts to match parallelism needs. Partition Key and Event Ordering means use a stable partition key such as deviceid to guarantee event order for related records; partitions themselves are the ordering domain.. In practical terms, how partition keys affect where events land and why ordering is preserved per partition. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Partition Key
What partition keys do
A partition key groups related events and routes them to the same partition so their relative order is preserved. The Event Hubs service hashes the key to pick a partition.
Concrete example
If device A sends events with partition key deviceA, those events will land in the same partition and consumers reading that partition will see them in order.
Misconception & planning
Partition keys do not guarantee ordering across different keys or across partitions. Also you cannot change partition count after creation. Plan keys and partition count with parallelism and ordering requirements in mind.
Key Takeaway
Use deviceId or another stable identifier as the partition key to maintain per-device ordering; size partitions to support expected parallel consumers.

screens.title: Consumer Patterns: EventHubConsumerClient and EventProcessorClient
screens.narratorSegment: Consumers read events from Event Hubs and apply business logic. There are two common patterns: using EventHubConsumerClient for simple consumption and EventProcessorClient for production workloads that need automatic load balancing and checkpointing. EventProcessorClient is the recommended approach when multiple instances run because it distributes partition ownership and coordinates checkpoint updates. Checkpointing records the offset of the last processed event to Azure Blob Storage so a restarted instance resumes where it left off. The provided consumer example shows an asynchronous on_event callback that prints event details and uses BlobCheckpointStore to persist offsets. A common pitfall is failing to checkpoint frequently enough or checkpointing in an expensive synchronous operation — this can cause duplicate processing or data loss on failure. As a concrete example, checkpoint after a fixed number of processed events or after committing an idempotent update to downstream storage. The closing question: how often will you checkpoint in your workload to balance performance and recovery speed? content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Consumer Patterns
Consumer example (concept)
from azure.eventhub.aio import EventHubConsumerClient
from azure.eventhub.extensions.checkpointstoreblobaio import BlobCheckpointStore

# Create BlobCheckpointStore from storage connection
checkpoint_store = BlobCheckpointStore.from_connection_string(
  AZURE_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STR,
  BLOB_CONTAINER_NAME
)

client = EventHubConsumerClient.from_connection_string(
  conn_str=EVENT_HUB_CONNECTION_STR,
  consumer_group=CONSUMER_GROUP,
  eventhub_name=EVENT_HUB_NAME,
  checkpoint_store=checkpoint_store
)

async def on_event(partition_context, event):
  # inspect event body and properties, then conditionally checkpoint
  await partition_context.update_checkpoint(event)

async with client:
  await client.receive(on_event=on_event, starting_position="-1")
This pattern uses BlobCheckpointStore so offsets are durable. EventProcessorClient builds on this to handle partition load balancing when multiple instances run concurrently.
Tips
  • Checkpoint after successful, idempotent processing or every N events.
  • Use consumer groups to isolate different consumer applications.
  • Monitor partition ownership and lag to detect imbalances.

screens.title: Checkpointing, Consumer Groups, and Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: Checkpointing, consumer groups, and partition ownership together form the reliability stack for Event Hubs consumers. A checkpoint records a consumer's last processed offset for a given partition and consumer group, typically stored in Blob Storage via BlobCheckpointStore. Consumer groups allow multiple independent consuming applications to read the same event stream without interfering. When you run multiple instances of the same consumer application, EventProcessorClient coordinates partition ownership and load balancing so each partition is processed by a single instance at a time. This prevents duplicate processing within the same consumer group. A typical architecture puts Blob storage as the checkpoint store and runs several instances behind an autoscaling group; when an instance fails, EventProcessorClient redistributes partition ownership to healthy instances. One common mistake is using the same consumer group for unrelated consumers; that causes contention and reduces throughput. Key takeaway: use consumer groups to isolate consumers, checkpoint to durable storage, and rely on EventProcessorClient to balance partitions across instances. Checkpointing, Consumer Groups, and Load Balancing means store checkpoints in blob storage, use consumer groups for independent consumers, and allow eventprocessorclient to manage partition ownership for scaling.. In practical terms, how checkpoints and consumer groups enable scalable, fault‑tolerant consumption. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Checkpointing & Load‑balancing
How it works
  • Checkpoint stores the last processed offset per partition and consumer group.
  • BlobCheckpointStore persists checkpoint metadata to a Storage container.
  • EventProcessorClient uses checkpoint data to claim ownership and balance partitions across instances.
Real example
Three consumer instances will each own some partitions; when one fails, the others rebalance and resume processing from checkpoints saved in Blob Storage.
Common mistakes & checks
  1. Using one consumer group for multiple unrelated apps — create separate consumer groups per logical consumer.
  2. Checkpointing too infrequently — balance throughput with recovery window.
  3. Not monitoring partition ownership — add telemetry to detect hot partitions.

screens.narratorSegment: Event Hubs Capture provides automatic archival of event streams to a designated Storage account or Data Lake Storage Gen2. When enabled on an Event Hub you choose a container and a capture format — Avro or Parquet — and define a time window or size threshold. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Event Hubs Capture
Capture configuration
Choose a Storage account and container, then select Avro or Parquet. Configure a capture window by time or size; when the trigger fires, a file is written automatically.
Why use Capture
Capture removes operational overhead required to build a custom archival consumer and guarantees raw event retention for batch processing.
Notes & misconception
Capture is an archival mechanism; it does not replace real-time consumers for analytics. Use Capture for raw data retention and a consumer for real-time processing.
Practical note
Files written by Capture are structured for downstream batch jobs. Choose Avro if you need schema evolution support, or Parquet for columnar analytics performance.

screens.title: Common Issues and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When working with Event Hubs, several recurring issues appear. First, sending small, single‑event requests instead of batches dramatically reduces throughput. The fix is to aggregate related events into a batch before sending. Second, failing to implement checkpointing leads to duplicate processing or data loss after a crash; address this by using BlobCheckpointStore or EventProcessorClient and checkpointing at safe points in your pipeline. Third, using a single consumer group for different consuming applications causes contention and reduces performance; create separate consumer groups per logical consumer. Fourth, hardcoding connection strings exposes secrets; move them to Key Vault or use managed identities. Finally, partition imbalance can create hot partitions; monitor partition load and consider re-partitioning by creating a new Event Hub with a higher partition count if needed. Each issue has observable signals — high RPC count, duplicated outputs, or uneven consumer lag. A practical debugging approach is to check metrics, validate consumer group usage, and verify checkpoint blobs in Storage. Closing question: which signal will you watch first in your pipeline to detect problems? Core Concept Troubleshooting
Problem: Unbatched sends
Symptoms: High RPC rate, low throughput. Fix: Aggregate events and send in batches to reduce overhead.
Problem: No checkpointing
Symptoms: Duplicate processing after restart. Fix: Use BlobCheckpointStore and checkpoint after safe commits.
Problem: Consumer group misuse
Symptoms: Contention and reduced throughput. Fix: Create separate consumer groups for independent consumers.
Debugging checklist
  • Inspect metrics for RPC calls, incoming events, and outgoing bytes.
  • Verify checkpoint blobs in your Storage container to confirm progress.
  • Confirm each logical consumer uses its own consumer group.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you’ll master practical techniques for sending and receiving streams with Azure Event Hubs. We’ll cover portal configuration so you have a namespace and an Event Hub ready, then build a Python producer that sends JSON payloads efficiently using batching and partition keys. You will also learn how to write a consumer that uses checkpointing and Blob storage so processing can resume after failures. We’ll explain EventProcessorClient and BlobCheckpointStore for load balanced, fault tolerant consumption, and how Event Hubs Capture archives raw events to Azure Storage in Avro or Parquet format. Throughout, I’ll show concrete examples, common mistakes to avoid — like sending tiny unbatched events or failing to checkpoint — and simple remedies. By the end you will understand the end-to-end flow from device telemetry to archive, why ordering matters for device streams, and how to make your consumers resilient. Think about one stream you will build: how will you guarantee ordering and restart safely after a crash?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure an Event Hubs namespace and create an Event Hub in the Azure portal so your applications have a secure endpoint. You will implement a Python producer that sends JSON‑formatted EventData in efficient batches and uses a partition key to preserve order for related records. You will also implement a consumer that reads events reliably, using checkpointing so processing resumes after failures; we’ll show how Blob storage works as the checkpoint store. You will enable Event Hubs Capture to archive raw events to a Storage account for later batch processing. Finally, you’ll be able to identify common ingestion and consumption issues, such as unbatched sends, improper checkpointing, and consumer group contention, and apply fixes. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can confirm your practical readiness for production streams.

These objectives are practical. Configuring the namespace determines partition count and throughput units which affect parallelism and limits. Writing a producer that batches events reduces network overhead and improves throughput; using the device identifier as the partition key keeps related events ordered. Building consumers that checkpoint to Blob storage or leverage the EventProcessorClient means your service can restart gracefully without duplicate processing. Enabling Capture reduces operational burden by automatically archiving raw streams in a durable file format for later batch processing. Finally, recognizing common mistakes like using a single consumer group for multiple independent consumers or storing connection strings in application code helps you design secure, scalable pipelines. Each skill you practice here maps to a real task in production deployments and measurable milestones you can verify during the hands-on activity.

Creating an Event Hubs namespace and an Event Hub in the portal is the foundation for reliable ingestion. Start by selecting or creating a resource group, then create an Event Hubs namespace; choose the pricing and throughput options that match expected traffic. When you create the Event Hub inside the namespace pick an appropriate partition count because partitions determine parallelism and ordering domains. A higher partition count allows more concurrent readers, but partitions are fixed after creation, so plan for future scaling. After provisioning, retrieve the namespace connection string from the Shared access policies section and copy it securely. For checkpointing you will also prepare a Storage account and container to hold checkpoint blobs. One common misconception is that partitions are dynamic— they are not; resizing requires a new Event Hub and data migration strategy. A concrete example: if a telemetry system will have many independent device streams that need parallel consumer processing, plan for several partitions; if ordering per device is required, use deviceId as a partition key rather than increasing partitions. Key takeaway: choose partitions and throughput with future scaling and ordering requirements in mind.

A connection string contains the endpoint and authentication credentials that let your producer and consumer talk to an Event Hub. It is convenient for development, but in production storing that string directly in code is a common security mistake. Instead, use Azure Key Vault to store secrets or, where supported, use a managed identity so your application requests tokens without handling raw keys. When you copy a connection string from the portal you will typically use a policy such as RootManageSharedAccessKey for testing, but production systems should use least privilege policies scoped to send or listen. As an example, a producer app can retrieve a connection string from Key Vault at startup and then open an EventHubProducerClient from that connection string. Another misconception is thinking managed identities replace all configuration; they replace secret storage but your application still needs the Event Hub name and consumer group configuration. Key takeaway: protect your connection information, rotate keys when needed, and apply least privilege for better security posture. Connection Strings, Security, and Best Practices means use key vault or managed identities; avoid embedding namespace keys in application code and prefer least-privilege policies.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This code walkthrough demonstrates a practical Python producer that sends telemetry events in batches. The producer opens an EventHubProducerClient from a connection string and creates EventData objects by serializing dictionaries to JSON. Best practice is to create batches with create_batch and add events to the batch before sending. Batching reduces per-event network overhead and improves throughput. The partition key is set so related events, for example those from the same deviceId, are guaranteed to land in the same partition and preserve ordering. A typical pattern simulates multiple devices and uses the device identifier as the partition key property. One misconception is setting partition keys on different events expecting cross-device ordering; partition keys only guarantee ordering within the same key value. In production, you should also handle retries and backoff and avoid blocking the event loop in async apps. Partition keys are the mechanism that routes related events to the same partition so they are processed in order. When you set a partition key, all events with the same key are guaranteed to be written to the same partition, maintaining sequence within that partition. This is essential for scenarios like device telemetry where the sequence of sensor readings matters. For example, using deviceId as a partition key ensures all events from a single device appear in arrival order on the same partition. A common misconception is that a partition key enforces global ordering across the Event Hub; it does not. Ordering is only guaranteed within a partition for identical partition keys. There are two common patterns: using EventHubConsumerClient for simple consumption and EventProcessorClient for production workloads that need automatic load balancing and checkpointing. EventProcessorClient is the recommended approach when multiple instances run because it distributes partition ownership and coordinates checkpoint updates. Checkpointing records the offset of the last processed event to Azure Blob Storage so a restarted instance resumes where it left off. Checkpointing, consumer groups, and partition ownership together form the reliability stack for Event Hubs consumers. Consumer groups allow multiple independent consuming applications to read the same event stream without interfering.
